title: Saltend Chemicals Park
text:
Motion made, and Question proposed, That this House do now adjourn.—(Claire Hughes.)

Graham Stuart (Beverley and Holderness) (Con): Saltend Chemicals Park, just outside Hull, is one of the most important industrial sites in East Yorkshire. It is owned and operated by the px Group. Across its 370 acres, companies including INEOS, the Mitsubishi Chemical Group, Triton Power, Air Products and Yara—though currently mothballed—make chemicals and provide the power, gases and services on which other businesses depend.

Saltend matters to the region, because it provides skilled technical jobs. It matters to British industry, because its companies supply one another and businesses far beyond the Humber. It matters to the country, because we need the capacity to make foundational chemicals here in Britain. Last year, Vivergo ceased producing bioethanol and animal feed at Saltend. The Government’s trade deal, unfortunately with Donald Trump, gave US ethanol tariff-free access to the UK market for 1.4 billion litres a year, equivalent to the size of the entire UK market. Vivergo was already struggling, but its owner said that after that deal its position was made untenable. The Government did not provide the solution needed to keep it open, and it shut, with £700 million of investment by a great British company, ABF, lost in the process. I said at the time that the Government had offered the British bioethanol industry to the Americans on a plate, and we saw the consequences at Saltend. We cannot, tonight, bring back the production lost at Vivergo, but we can act while there is still time to save the INEOS plants.

Three INEOS chemicals plants at Saltend have stopped production. All 245 staff remain employed, and the plants and the skills are still there. The time to save them is now. Those jobs matter enormously, but the country also stands to lose something harder to replace: the capacity to make these foundational chemicals. At Saltend, INEOS makes acetic acid, acetic anhydride and ethyl acetate, which are used in the production of medicines, food preservatives, packaging, ink and adhesives, to name just a few. Most of us, of course, will never see those chemicals themselves, but we see and rely on the products made with them.

If we lose the capacity to produce those chemicals here, British industry will become more dependent on supplies from overseas. That is a question of industrial resilience and, ultimately, national security. The Government rightly say that they want to reindustrialise and, in particular, to reindustrialise the north, and I want the Government to succeed, but keeping the industry that we already have is the first test of that ambition.

INEOS is an anchor tenant at Saltend Chemicals Park. That phrase can sound abstract, so let me explain what it means. Businesses there share services, power and steam: what one company produces, another one uses. They invest on the basis that the park works as a whole, with people working together. I have spoken to Mitsubishi Chemical about the effect of INEOS’s stopped production on its operation and investment. It is midway through a £500 million investment there, which is now on pause. I have spoken to Triton Power, which supplies electricity and steam to the park. When industrial demand falls, the economics of providing those services change too. Neither company told me that it was about to close, or would be forced to close by the INEOS shutdown. What they showed me was that the loss of an anchor tenant would be felt well beyond that anchor tenant’s business.

About 800 highly skilled and highly paid people work across Saltend Chemicals Park, with thousands more in the supply chain. I do not suggest that every one of those jobs is immediately at risk, but the park’s future as a place for skilled technical work depends on keeping its businesses connected and investing. A decision that appears to concern those three INEOS plants could shape what happens on the other plants across the site for years to come. That is why I ask the Minister to look beyond the immediate payroll, important though that is. Once a chemicals plant closes permanently and its workforce disperses, we cannot simply decide later that we would like to get that capability back. We would have to rebuild the skills, the industrial relationships and the confidence to invest.

title: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
text:
Madam Deputy Speaker (Judith Cummins): I draw the House’s attention to the fact that financial privilege is engaged by Lords amendments 48 to 52 and 54. If any of these Lords amendments is agreed to, I will cause the customary entry for the waiving of Commons financial privilege to be made in the Journal.

After Clause 58

Review of the effectiveness of the NIS regime

The Minister for Creative Industries, Media and Online Safety (Ian Murray): I beg to move, That this House disagrees with Lords amendment 107.

Madam Deputy Speaker: With this it will be convenient to discuss:

Lords amendment 108, and Government motion to disagree.

Lords amendments 1 to 32.

Lords amendment 33, and amendments (a) to (i).

Lords amendments 34 to 106 and 109 to 112.

Ian Murray: It is a pleasure to bring this important Bill, which has cross-party support, back to the House. Lords amendment 107 would require the Secretary of State to undertake a comprehensive annual review of the effectiveness of the network and information systems regime. Many issues are raised by this amendment, and I consider the Government to have listened and responded to them carefully.

First, the Bill already requires a post-implementation review of the regime. Following concerns raised in the other place, the Government tabled Lords amendment 42 to reduce the timeframe of the review from every five years to every three years. That will allow us to undertake a meaningful and more timely review.

Secondly, we have listened to concerns about the sectors in scope of the regime. In the other place, the Minister for Space, Cyber and Regulatory Reform made a clear commitment at the Dispatch Box to assess whether critical sectors not already in scope should be part of the regime and report back to Parliament within 12 months of Royal Assent. I can commit to going further. I confirm that the Government will table an amendment when the Bill goes back to the other place to this effect, so that it is on the face of the Bill. To allow for a flexible approach, it will require the Secretary of State to lay a statement within 12 months of the passage of the Bill, setting out which further activities should be specified as essential under this regime. I can commit that, to inform this statement, the Secretary of State will consider whether activities and services within the UK’s critical national infrastructure sectors should be brought within scope of the regime. I can also commit that we will go further and consider advanced manufacturing, electoral infrastructure and political parties within 24 months of Royal Assent.

Sir John Hayes (South Holland and The Deepings) (Con): The Minister is showing responsiveness and flexibility, and I think he understands that, although the Bill does enjoy cross-party support, there is a need to get it right. Part of that is recognising that this is a highly dynamic environment and that technology moves very fast. What is probably in the their lordships’ minds is that that requires a very regular reappraisal of the appropriateness of the application of policy. To that end—I raised this point last week when we debated artificial intelligence—I wonder whether the Minister might look at the whole issue of interoperability and interconnectivity. My fear is that we are concentrating risk, and when we review these matters we might want to consider that in a cross-departmental way.

title: Armed Forces Bill
text:
[Relevant documents: First Special Report of the Select Committee on the Armed Forces Bill of Session 2024-26, Armed Forces Bill 2026, HC 1712; oral evidence taken before the Select Committee on the Armed Forces Bill, on Armed Forces Bill 2026, 4 March and 3 March, Session 2024-26, HC 1712.]

Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani): I draw the House’s attention to the fact that financial privilege is engaged by Lords amendments 2, 15 and 18. If any of those Lords amendments are agreed to, I will cause the customary entry for the waiving of Commons financial privilege to be made in the Journal.

After Clause 3

Military homes standard

The Minister for the Armed Forces (Louise Sandher-Jones): I beg to move, That this House disagrees with Lords amendment 2.

Madam Deputy Speaker: With this it will be convenient to discuss:

Lords amendment 18, and Government motion to disagree.

Lords amendments 11 and 25, Government motion to disagree, and Government amendments (a) to (r) to the words so restored to the Bill.

Lords amendments 1, 3 to 10, 12 to 17 and 19 to 24.

Louise Sandher-Jones: The Government invite the House to agree with Lords amendment 1, 3 to 10, 12 to 17 and 19 to 24, which we tabled in the other place. We invite the House to disagree with Lords amendments 2 and 18, which were proposed by Baroness Smith of Newnham, and with Lords amendments 11 and 25, which were proposed by the Opposition. In disagreeing with Lords amendments 11 and 25, we will propose Government amendments to the restored Reserve Forces and Cadets Association provisions to the Bill.

Lords amendments 1 and 3 to 7 respond to recommendations made by the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee. The Government considered the Committee’s recommendations carefully, and the amendments simply ensure an appropriate level of parliamentary scrutiny for both the armed forces covenant statutory guidance and the code for victims in the service justice system. Lords amendments 8 and 9 ensure that the provisions enabling transfers between the regular and reserve forces operate as intended. Lords amendment 10 modernises the way in which reservists can be contacted by allowing call-out and recall notices to be served by email.

Lords amendments 12 to 14, 16 and 17 make provision in relation to assaults against members of the service police and create an offence of impersonating a member of the service police. Lords amendment 15 concerns immigration fees for eligible armed forces personnel and their families. It requires regulations to provide for specified fee exemptions, which I confirm will be implemented before the end of September 2027.

Ben Obese-Jecty (Huntingdon) (Con): I wholeheartedly support Lords amendment 15 on the issue of immigration fees for Commonwealth personnel. Having brought two amendments to the House, which sadly were voted down, I am reassured that the Government have accepted the Lords amendment so that we can finally get this pushed through and Commonwealth veterans can receive the support that they need for their families.

title: Funeral Directors etc (Register)
text:
Motion for leave to bring in a Bill (Standing Order No. 23)

Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani): Before we come to the ten-minute rule motion, I should inform the House that the case relating to Elkin and Bell Funerals has been referred to the Court of Appeal by the Attorney General under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, and it is therefore sub judice. Mr Speaker has granted a waiver to allow the case to be referred to during this debate. The facts of the case and the convictions may be referred to, but Members may not discuss the sentencing review or matters that might influence sentencing decisions, such as the seriousness of the offences or the length of the sentences originally imposed.

Dame Caroline Dinenage (Gosport) (Con): I beg to move,

That leave be given to bring in a Bill to require the Secretary of State to prepare and maintain a register of funeral directors, private mortuaries, direct cremation services and certain other persons who transport or hold the bodies of deceased persons; and for connected purposes.

It has been three years since I first met Ministers to register my horror, because I had just discovered that anybody—no matter their background, expertise or resources—could set up business as a funeral director. Since then, there have been numerous meetings and numerous Ministers; the Government have said a lot and done almost nothing. The disturbing fact remains that in the funeral industry, there is no minimum qualification, no registration, no licensing, no inspection, no formal regulation and, crucially, no dedicated legislation to fall back on when things go wrong. In fact, the funeral sector is almost completely unregulated. Of course, this matter remains as pressing as ever.

Last December, Gosport funeral directors Richard Elkin and Hayley Bell were convicted after a court heard they had kept 46 bodies on their business premises in an unrefrigerated room. Bailiffs entering the premises found two bodies stored without refrigeration in a dilapidated room with water leaking through the ceiling. One of those bodies—that of an elderly gentleman who had been left for 36 days—was badly decomposed.

Elkin and Bell were brought to justice only by using a jigsaw of non-purpose-built legislation, including the offence of carrying on business with an attempt to defraud, causing a public nuisance, and a Victorian common-law offence of preventing a lawful burial that dates back to the times of the grave robbers. Imagine the hurt of those families who believed that the body of their loved one had been properly cared for, respectfully placed into a coffin and cremated with dignity, only to find that instead it had been left to rot on a rack at the back of the funeral parlour—it is almost unimaginable.

We put enormous, unquestioning trust in those who care for the bodies of our loved ones when they die. There have been a number of high-profile cases across the UK, but in the case of Elkin and Bell, 46 grieving families were robbed of a proper grieving process because they had been left to worry about how their relatives’ bodies were mishandled. That is before we talk about those left wondering whether there were others besides those 46.

I have therefore been calling for the Government to urgently bring forward proposals to establish a proper framework of regulation around the death pathway. The real horror is that this will not be an isolated case—it could be happening out there in our communities as I speak. Under the law as it stands today, anyone can set themselves up as a funeral director without any meaningful supervision.

The Fuller inquiry, whose report was published in July last year, made five recommendations to the Government. Almost a year and a half later, the promised response has not arrived. Those recommendations were quite simple: first, that

“The UK government should establish an independent statutory regulatory regime for funeral directors in England”;

secondly, that

“These regulations and standards should be considered within the overall care and journey of the deceased”;

thirdly, that

“mandatory information be given to customers by funeral directors to provide transparency about the care of the deceased”;

fourthly, that

“Direct cremation businesses should also be considered”

as part of the reforms; and fifthly, that

“the benefit to customers and the need for public confidence outweigh the difficulties that may be experienced by some

title: COP31
text:
The Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero (Miatta Fahnbulleh): With permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to make a statement following the conclusion of the COP31 climate summit. This year’s climate conference sought to confront a hard truth: that the world is on course to exceed 1.5° of warming by around 2030. We all know what this will mean for communities at home and abroad. At around 1.4° of warming today, we are already seeing the impacts.

Here in Britain, this summer brought record heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, and it was people’s homes, their livelihoods and the communities that they love that were impacted. And not just that: lives were lost, too. As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care informed the House earlier, the UK Health Security Agency released data today showing that we saw a total of 5,258 heat-related deaths in the UK over 2026. We cannot stand by and let this be the new normal.

Overseas, we saw the devastation on the Nepal-China border with heartbreaking scenes of communities destroyed. Around the world, communities on the frontline of the climate crisis are seeing their homes destroyed and their livelihoods threatened. Climate change is here, and as we overshoot 1.5°, the impacts will be felt in country after country, the world over. So I went to COP31 clear about the challenge we face, and about the urgency of taking climate action. The target of 1.5° remains the right target. As the UN Secretary-General has said, overshoot does not mean surrender; it means redoubling our efforts. We arrived in Antalya determined to work with our partners to reach consensus on the need for urgent, ambitious action.

COP31 delivered important progress across the wider negotiations, especially through the action agenda, but as the House knows, parties were unable to reach consensus on the cover decision. After concerted negotiations and tireless efforts to up the ambition, the substance that was proposed in the final cover decision did not meet the moment and we were unwilling to support it. It moved us backwards on the science when we needed to move faster. It failed to reaffirm our existing collective commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and our commitment to keep 1.5° within reach. It compromised where we needed bold collective ambition, and I was immensely disappointed by this outcome.

We were not alone in standing up for these issues. We stood alongside small island developing states and some of the least developed countries on the very frontline of this crisis, which could not accept this as an adequate outcome. Now we have a responsibility to uphold and protect the Paris agreement. We have a duty to protect communities here in the UK, across the Commonwealth and in the countries most vulnerable to climate shocks.

Although we could not find consensus on the cover decision, COP31 saw success beyond this. We worked with partners around the world and made progress that was not reflected in the proposed cover text. The technical negotiations delivered progress on areas including the global goal on adaptation and just transition. Conferences of the parties are increasingly about turning commitments into action through the action agenda, which was a significant focus for the Turkish COP presidency. We saw the strongest ever backing for mobilising action, with 119 countries using the closing event to recognise the wider implementation that is happening. That is concrete progress, and it demonstrates the global momentum for the energy transition.

I am proud of the UK’s role in this effort. More than ever, it has strengthened our commitment to multilateralism and our resolve to work with partners in every region of the world to drive action ahead of COP32. I want to thank the UK’s negotiating team, led by Kate Hughes, and everyone across the UK civil service, business and civil society who contributed to this effort. I have seen at first hand their dedication, hard work and determination to make progress. Together we focused our efforts on five areas: electrification and clean energy; methane; forests and oceans; finance; and resilience.

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text:
The Minister for Social Security and Disability (Sir Stephen Timms): With permission, I would like to make a statement on the final report of the Timms review of the personal independence payment. PIP provides vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long-term health conditions. It contributes to the additional costs they face, and aims to help them to live independently, to participate in their communities and often to work.

PIP was introduced 13 years ago. Since then, lots has changed, but PIP has never been fully reviewed, and it has not kept pace, so the Timms review was launched in summer last year. The review was co-produced with disabled people, the organisations that represent them and other experts. It is the first time that the UK Government have co-produced a review of this scale. I express heartfelt thanks to my two co-chairs, Sharon Brennan and Dr Clenton Farquharson, and to the 12 steering group members, whom the three of us recruited from more than 340 applicants. The group has met for a full day on 15 occasions since January, with lots of other discussions in between. The whole group has shown exemplary commitment to the task.

Each of the 15 members, including me, had one vote. Almost all 12 of the steering group members had lived experience of disability or long-term ill health, as well as a range of other expertise. The review heard from more than 40,000 people and organisations, including more than 38,000 responses to the call for evidence, 138 community workshops, and evidence from clinicians, charities, deaf and disabled people’s organisations, academics, frontline practitioners and international experts. I thank everyone who shared their expertise and their experiences—often very personal ones—with us.

This was an ambitious review, and it asked big, complex questions. Co-production means that every participant does not necessarily agree on every detail, but we created the conditions for people with different perspectives to test the evidence and shape the outcome as equals. The review’s report has been submitted to my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State, and the Government will now consider its findings.

I will turn to the review’s central conclusion: the system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset. The review is clear that PIP remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It does not consider people’s needs, aspirations, barriers or extra costs—it is just about what someone cannot do. Many find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and too often it leaves people fearing that work, health treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it.

Secondly, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution towards the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey, reviewed by the steering group, showed that PIP does not always target the highest levels of support at those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions better reflecting individual circumstances.

Thirdly, the system offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.

The review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not just some adjustment of the form or descriptors. It does not prescribe a final set of eligibility rules, because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected Government, accountable to this House, but it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made. Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly. The highest support should reflect the most severe needs. A good deal of further work is needed. The Government will undertake this work, and we will set out our plans in next year’s White Paper.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text:
Richard Tice (Boston and Skegness) (Reform): To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office to make a statement on the UK civil service pension scheme and the performance of Capita plc.

The Parliamentary Secretary, Cabinet Office (Sally Jameson): Before I begin my response, I declare that I have a Capita pension from the Prison Service under the civil service pension scheme.

We are aware of the announcement that Capita issued to the market yesterday, including on the appointment of its new chief executive officer, Pablo Andres. The Government routinely monitor the financial health of our strategic suppliers. It would not be appropriate for us to comment on the wider commercial position of Capita as a company, as that is a commercial matter for Capita and its shareholders.

Capita’s performance on the pension scheme has had unacceptable impacts on people who have dedicated years of their working lives to serving this country, and they deserve better. We are using the most stringent commercial levers, including requiring deliverable plans and withholding payments under the contract that was signed under the last Government. To hold Capita to account, we mandated that it appoint an independent remedial adviser at its own expense. The report identified many weaknesses in Capita’s rectification planning, from technology implementation to its overall ambition, which fell well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve.

To address that, I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with it to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account. Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita’s systems and data to provide us with firmer assurance of the accuracy of the management information and to allow even stronger challenge on Capita’s direction and performance. I have put in place dedicated teams to work alongside Capita to agree priorities, improve quality and processes, and ensure that pensions are paid correctly.

The new recovery plan is made up of five workstreams. They cover casework across every level of complexity, major statutory exercises, including the McCloud remedy, and the underlying technology and infrastructure needed to fix delivery. Rightly, we have required Capita to prioritise the oldest cases first, tackling the root causes in those legacy cases, and that is already unblocking similar queries across the system. That is why Capita is now issuing more quotes for complex cases that are less than three months old. Simultaneously, members with complex cases are now supported by a dedicated team and a specialist helpline. For non-complex cases, including retirement quotes, we have seen some improvement and, as I announced in my recent statement, there is now a fortnightly dashboard where members can view progress.

Although that is some progress, there remains a lot more to do, and there are still too many people waiting on the pensions they are owed. I will continue to hold Capita’s management team to account and apply the strongest possible commercial levers under the contract to rectify the situation for those who still have not received the service that Capita should have already delivered.

title: Topical Questions
text:
Callum Anderson (Buckingham and Bletchley) (Lab): T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.

The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Yvette Cooper): This morning the UK Health Security Agency published new figures showing that 5,258 people died this summer due to extreme heat. That is three quarters higher than the previous record in 2022, and it is well over double the number of winter deaths last year. I offer my deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer.

The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, which is why I have asked the NHS to prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter, and why we have our new heat taskforce and an initial £32 million to provide better cooling and ventilation in hospitals. The unprecedented summer has increased the challenges for the NHS for the winter, so we are also investing £1.9 billion over several years in urgent and emergency care facilities, with 25 new and expanded urgent care schemes and centres open or due to become operational this winter, alongside the support for GPs to help care for people at home.

Callum Anderson: Next Monday, after a decade of campaigning by local people, the new Lace Hill health centre in Buckingham will finally open its doors to patients, and I pay tribute to the Swan Health team for all their work in getting this over the line. When I met them recently, one of the issues that they raised was their ability to hire the GPs and nurses that they need. Does my right hon. Friend have an update on how she is working with GP practices to ensure that they have the workforce they need?

Yvette Cooper: I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Swan Health and Dr George Gavriel, who works at the practice. I also congratulate my hon. Friend on the role that he has played in campaigning and arguing for investment in this new, modern facility, which is so important to the community. We have already increased the number of fully qualified GPs by 10% over the past two years and, as a result of the work that we have done, there are 24 million additional GP appointments. My hon. Friend rightly points to the importance of the workforce, and we will continue to support them.

Dr Caroline Johnson (Sleaford and North Hykeham) (Con): First, may I thank the Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety for correcting the record after our last Health and Social Care questions? Now that the Government are aware that people are waiting so long in A&E, I hope that we can see some improvements. Waiting lists more generally are rising and have been since Easter, and for those waiting for a procedure or an operation, the waiting list is higher than it was last month, last year and since the general election. Is the Secretary of State aware of that, and what is she going to do about it?

Yvette Cooper: I can tell the hon. Member that 615,000 fewer patients are waiting over 18 weeks for non-urgent hospital treatment as a result of the improvements in elective performance since the general election. We have instigated a major turnaround programme after the Conservative party took this country from the lowest ever waiting lists to the highest ever waiting lists.

Kate Osborne (Jarrow and Gateshead East) (Lab): T3. This month, the all-party parliamentary group on fertility called for a national fertility strategy. We have heard about the realities and problems of accessing treatment, including the additional barriers faced by same-sex couples who have to pay privately for donor insemination before being considered on the NHS. Does the Minister agree with me that this gay tax must finally be ended, and will she meet me to discuss a national fertility strategy?

The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety (Dame Diana Johnson): I pay tribute to my hon. Friend for her work as chair of the APPG on fertility, and I know that she has been raising a number of these issues for some time. As I set out in my earlier answers, work is under way to look at what is going on with ICBs at the moment, but I am of course always very happy to meet Members.

title: Diethylstilbestrol: Support for Affected Women
text:
Jessica Toale (Bournemouth West) (Lab): 14. What steps her Department is taking to support women affected by diethylstilbestrol.

The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety (Dame Diana Johnson): May I start by paying tribute to my hon. Friend for all her work on DES and for representing her constituent Jan Hall? My hon. Friend raised this issue at our last oral questions, and I can confirm that the review with the University of Exeter is moving forward, with the publication of protocols setting out how the research will be conducted. Its findings will then be reviewed by a clinical steering group, and will inform decisions on screening and guidance.

Jessica Toale: I thank the Minister for her answer. It appears that there is still no mammogram screening pathway for DES-exposed women, who are 30 times more likely to get breast cancer. These women require routine screening far before the age of 50. What steps has the Department taken since I last raised the issue of enhanced access and screening for DES-linked cancers?

Dame Diana Johnson: My hon. Friend is right to raise this issue. To improve clinical awareness, the notice to cancer alliance directors was reissued on 26 October to ensure that affected women are identified and supported, in line with the existing guidance. My officials are engaging with NHS England on concerns about the guidance on DES not being easily accessible, and I would very much welcome a meeting with my hon. Friend and campaigners to hear directly about what more we can do.

Jim Shannon (Strangford) (DUP): I thank the Minister for her answers, and I thank the hon. Member for Bournemouth West (Jessica Toale) for bringing forward the question and outlining the dangers of DES, which was used from the ’40s to the ’70s. It is still being used in exceptional circumstances, but if there is a proven history of disease and people will unfortunately lose their lives, is it not the case that it should never be used?

Dame Diana Johnson: I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for making that point. My understanding is that DES is not being used, but I will go away and seek advice from officials about that. Clearly, clinical decisions are made, but I will certainly get an answer for the hon. Gentleman.

title: Employers: Ill Health Prevention
text:
Kim Leadbeater (Spen Valley) (Lab): 13. What steps she is taking with the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions to support employers to prevent ill health.

The Minister for Social Care and Mental Health (Alison McGovern): Being able to work can be every bit as vital to our health as any treatment that we receive, which is why, alongside all the work being done by our colleagues in the Department for Work and Pensions, we are supporting access to talking therapies and to the healthcare that matters most for participation in work. Prevention starts with young people. Professor Fonagy’s review showed that there is more to do, and we will soon publish a new mental health strategy responding to the issues that he identified.

Kim Leadbeater: In 2023, when I sat on the Opposition Benches, I wrote a report called “Healthy Britain”, which set out a framework for a cross-Government, cross-sector approach to the health of the nation, with a particular focus on prevention and early intervention and a holistic approach to physical, mental and social wellbeing. I am delighted that the Labour Government have focused more on this agenda, but what are the Government doing to turbocharge that work so that, when possible, we can prevent people from becoming sick in the first place and build a strong, healthy nation with the many benefits—including, of course, economic benefits—that that brings?

Alison McGovern: I thank my hon. Friend both for the work that she did in opposition and for her continued championing of this issue. We have much more to do to create a healthier Britain, and she will have heard the comments of the Prime Minister and the Chancellor on the subject of prevention. This matters nowhere more than in mental health, and, as I have said, we will soon publish our strategy, which has been supported by colleagues across Government, including the Department for Education in respect of children’s mental health and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport in respect of participation.

Gideon Amos (Taunton and Wellington) (LD): Some of the most important work to help employers to prevent ill health in my constituency is carried out by the NHS veterans outreach service. Does the Minister agree that the reorganisation that has taken place in the NHS should not mean that those key personnel lose their jobs, and may I pay tribute to the campaigner Steve Summers, a Wellington veteran who has campaigned indefatigably to prevent those services from being cut?

Alison McGovern: That work sounds incredibly important, and I am sure that the decision makers in the hon. Gentleman’s area will have heard what he has said.

title: National Care Service
text:
Neil Duncan-Jordan (Poole) (Lab): 12. What steps she is taking to create a national care service.

The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Yvette Cooper): The Prime Minister set out a vision for a national care service and Baroness Casey’s independent commission will recommend next summer how that should be taken forward. In the meantime, we are already taking important steps to strengthen support for unpaid carers and the social care workforce. Last week, as a down payment on the national care service, I announced how neighbourhood support teams would start coming together to support the most frail and vulnerable people in our communities.

Neil Duncan-Jordan: I thank the Secretary of State for her answer, but does she agree that the best model for the national care service is one that is free at the point of delivery, just like the NHS, and funded by society as a whole, rather than through an adjusted triple lock?

Yvette Cooper: The Prime Minister has set out a plan for free personal care, and that should have alongside it an adjustment to the triple lock, where pensioners will still see their pensions go up in line with inflation or by 2.5%. Pensions will also track wages. That is the right thing to do. The adjustment will also allow us to provide a better deal for elderly people, who currently face such huge pressures from social care bills in old age.

Joe Robertson (Isle of Wight East) (Con): Delivering care to 50,000 people in urban Manchester is very different from the challenges of delivering care to 50,000 people in rural Cornwall or the Isle of Wight, which Policy Exchange calls “The Rural Penalty”. Does the Secretary of State accept that the system must be designed, and funded, to meet genuine challenges of geography, travel time and local need, rather than being based on population numbers alone?

Yvette Cooper: The health service does need to respond to different communities and different conditions, in rural Britain and in coastal areas. As the hon. Member will know, that was reflected in the chief medical officer’s recent report, and we take it extremely seriously. We want more devolution so that we can ensure services are most effectively designed for the communities where people live. Neighbourhood support teams will be providing support at home rather than expecting people to travel long distances for care or health support.

Dr Neil Shastri-Hurst (Solihull West and Shirley) (Con): We are, of course, still awaiting much of the detail of the Prime Minister’s proposed national care service. However, the Secretary of State must surely accept that if a third of people with dementia remain undiagnosed and many others with complex conditions are not yet accessing services, the £18 billion a year estimate for such a service is highly unlikely to reflect the true level of unmet need, and the eventual cost of the scheme will almost certainly be significantly higher than that advertised.

Yvette Cooper: I look forward to the cross-party talks with the hon. Member, and I hope we can build some consensus on the need to create a national care service. Families across Britain have been let down for far too long, partly because political parties and Governments have turned away from this difficult issue rather than asking themselves, “What practical steps can we take? What can we do, step by step, with, for instance, the social care workforce and the neighbourhood support teams, to build services that better reflect today’s needs?”

title: Waiting Times: Medway
text:
Tristan Osborne (Chatham and Aylesford) (Lab): 10. What steps she is taking to help reduce waiting times for elective and emergency treatment in Medway.

The Minister for Secondary Care (Karin Smyth): I thank my hon. Friend for meeting me recently with other hon. Friends to discuss the trust. I commend his work in supporting it. Whether it is elective or emergency care, we want all patients seen as quickly as possible. Despite record pressures for emergency care, more patients are being seen within four hours. In Kent and Medway, we have improved performance on the 18-week target from 59.8% to 63.9%, so more people are being seen more quickly. We are determined to improve performance further in Medway and across the country.

Tristan Osborne: I thank the Minister for meeting us last week to listen to our concerns. Under the previous Government, accident and emergency waiting times soared. There has been increasing demand across the country, including queues at my local Medway Maritime hospital just yesterday. What more can be done to share best practice, including for improved corridor care, so that we do not see repeats of those queues going into the future?

Karin Smyth: I thank my hon. Friend for the work he is doing with the trust. The trust is working alongside NHS England to use oversight and expertise to improve conditions for patients and staff. There are also the many measures we have introduced to improve flow of patients from contacting primary care through the entire system. We will continue to do that to see sustained progress. His area has had some long-standing challenges that go back many years. We are committed, along with him and other hon. Members, to ensuring that that progress is sustained.

title: Support for Carers
text:
Rachel Blake (Cities of London and Westminster) (Lab/Co-op): 9. What steps she is taking to increase support for carers.

The Minister for Social Care and Mental Health (Alison McGovern): Carers and unpaid family carers will be at the heart of our national care service. We will publish a five-point plan for the social care workforce next month, setting out immediate steps to improve recruitment, retention and retirement and building on the announcements we have already made on fair pay and pensions. Last week, we were delighted to announce the appointment of my hon. Friend the Member for Shipley (Anna Dixon) as the Government’s champion for unpaid family carers. She will work directly with unpaid carers and support the continued delivery of the unpaid carers action plan, as well as shaping the new national care service.

Rachel Blake: I thank the Minister for that update. Last week I met a constituent who is the sole carer for her 56-year-old brother as well as for her elderly parents. She also organises Dancing with Dementia, a wonderful service in Westminster. I work closely with City Carers Community in the City of London, who are unpaid carers for their loved ones. I hear what the Minister has said about workforce planning, and I would be grateful for her comments on how we will be supporting the assessment process for care needs. That is something that many unpaid carers struggle with, and I know the Government want to see action taken.

Alison McGovern: I thank my hon. Friend for her question and—through her, if I may—thank the organisations she mentioned, which do great work with carers. On assessments, part of our work is to support social workers and others, to ensure we have the workforce we need as we move towards the national care service. I would be very happy to discuss that further with my hon. Friend.

Mr Speaker: I call the Chair of the Health and Social Care Committee.

Layla Moran (Oxford West and Abingdon) (LD): The Minister will be aware of the tragic case of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who did not get the support she needed after telling her social worker that she was having suicidal thoughts. After my hon. Friend the Member for Stratford-on-Avon (Manuela Perteghella) raised that case at Prime Minister’s questions, the Prime Minister committed to mandatory suicide prevention training for frontline social workers. It was the lack of that training that let Matilda down, yet a freedom of information request by her brother Joel has revealed that only three local authorities in the country are making it mandatory. With 41% of parent-carers at some point having thoughts of taking their own lives, will the Minister meet me and my hon. Friend so that we can discuss every opportunity to make good on the Prime Minister’s promise?

Alison McGovern: I thank the Chair of the Select Committee for that very important question. I will of course meet her, and I will also raise that point with Professor Louis Appleby, who leads our advisory group on suicide prevention. As we refresh the national suicide prevention strategy, we need to incorporate this important work.

Anna Dixon (Shipley) (Lab): I am hugely grateful to my hon. Friend the Minister and to the Secretary of State for the opportunity to represent the 6 million unpaid family carers in Government. I look forward to working with my hon. Friend and with hon. Members across the House to champion unpaid carers in this place.

My hon. Friend will know that last week, Carers UK published its “State of Caring” survey. That survey identified that about one in three carers are not known to their GPs, so will she work with me to improve identification of carers by GPs and across the NHS?

Alison McGovern: I thank my hon. Friend for agreeing to take on her role—I know that all the unpaid family carers up and down the country will be at the top of her mind and at the heart of the work she is doing as we build the national care service. We ought to think about identification in the context of the remarks that the Secretary of State just made about protecting frail older people better. We cannot care for people unless we care for those who care for them.

title: NHS Maternity Services
text:
Victoria Collins (Harpenden and Berkhamsted) (LD): 7. What steps she is taking to improve NHS maternity services.

Rachel Gilmour (Tiverton and Minehead) (LD): 8. What steps she is taking to improve NHS maternity services.

The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Yvette Cooper): The Health Bill, currently passing through Parliament, will include provisions for a new maternity and neonatal commissioner to help drive up standards, and shortly we will publish the first action plan based on the work of the maternity and neonatal taskforce. Every family deserves the very best start in life.

Victoria Collins: My constituent, Megan, is expecting her third baby, usually a cause for celebration, but she is scared. She has seen maternity care fail and watched her midwife break down in tears. That is sadly no surprise, with three quarters of midwives having considered leaving in the past year and 80% feeling that their unit is not safely staffed. Will the Minister commit to better supporting midwives, including Lib Dem calls for 52 hours of protected paid training for every midwife every year?

Yvette Cooper: Support for the workforce is a critical part of the work we are doing through the taskforce. We are considering introducing a new modern services framework, a set of national standards for maternity and neonatal care. When I was a Health Minister 25 years ago, we were introducing national standards around maternity care. Those were cancelled and dropped, so it is important to introduce new standards now.

Rachel Gilmour: My constituents in west Somerset are served primarily by North Devon district hospital and Musgrove Park hospital, yet North Devon hospital’s maternity unit remains closed and Musgrove continues to face significant pressures. For families in some of the most remote communities on Exmoor, including villages and hamlets such as Porlock and Culbone, the nearest consultant-led maternity care can be more than an hour away by road. Does the Minister accept that it cannot be right in modern Britain that expectant mothers risk giving birth on the side of a B road because maternity services are too distant to reach safely? Will the Government act now to end this unacceptable situation?

Yvette Cooper: I agree that it is deeply unfair on families that North Devon maternity services continue to be closed. NHS England is meeting daily with the trust leadership to provide support and to ensure progress. The trust has been working on different ways to seek to recruit the additional staff it needs to keep services safe, because fundamentally the problem comes down to issues around recruitment. It has been offering additional financial incentives for relocation. We will continue to support the trust and to maintain that pressure and work in order to get those services safely opened, as rapidly as possible.

Damien Egan (Bristol North East) (Lab): In April, the Royal College of Midwives commissioned a review into its workplace culture. Unlike a similar review by the Royal College of Nursing, the findings and recommendations have not been made public. If the review has not already been shared, is the Secretary of State able to confirm that she will request sight of the recommendations and seek assurances that they will be acted on?

Yvette Cooper: I can tell my hon. Friend that we work with all the royal colleges on what improvements need to be made, but issues around culture and the need to have really effective multidisciplinary teams and workforce teams as part of maternity services are crucial. That is part of what we are looking at through the maternity taskforce.

Gregory Stafford (Farnham and Bordon) (Con): Maternity readmissions within six weeks of birth have risen by more than a third in just three years, and data shows that at least one in five baby deaths last year may have been preventable. In June, the Government promised a maternity and neonatal commissioner; nearly six months on, no one has been appointed. How many avoidable tragedies have to occur before this Secretary of State gets a grip on maternity services?

title: Representation of the People Bill
text:
68: After Clause 38, insert the following new Clause— “Compulsory voting(1) The Secretary of State must, within six months of the day on which section 17 comes into force, publish and lay before both Houses of Parliament proposals for introducing a compulsory duty to vote at UK parliamentary elections and local elections in England for individuals who are registered to vote.(2) Proposals published under this section relating to compulsory voting must include— (a) provision for electors to be able to mark an abstention, either through returning a spoilt or blank ballot,(b) provision for the failure to vote to be punishable through a penalty fine of £10,(c) provision for certain exemptions to be made for those who are prevented from participating in an election, including—(i) those with a physical or mental incapacity, illness, or disability,(ii) those who are absent from the UK, and(iii) those with a sincerely held conscientious or religious belief, and(d) provision for pilots of compulsory voting in connection with any pilots undertaken under section 20.”Member’s explanatory statement This new clause seeks to require the Secretary of State to bring forward proposals for compulsory voting, including piloting compulsory voting in connection with any pilots of changes to voter registration process.

Baroness Royall of Blaisdon (Lab): My Lords, Amendments 68 and 121 in this group are in my name. I indicated at Second Reading that I would move an amendment on compulsory voting, which I believe is a proven method of increasing voter turnout at elections, ensuring that citizens use their vote to influence the shape of our country, and empowering them to bring about change. I am grateful to my noble friends Lord Foulkes, Lord Blunkett and Lord Kinnock, who could not be here this evening, but who strongly support this amendment. I thank my noble friend the Minister for referring to this in her letter to all Peers, dated 14 October, in which she spoke of the focus on removing barriers to participation and making it easier for eligible electors to register and vote.

I welcome the Government’s open-minded approach and their support, through the democratic engagement fund, of projects that help people understand and engage in democracy, and that will help build the evidence base on the most effective way of increasing democratic participation. This is very good, and I hope my noble friend will direct the fund to evaluate mandatory turnout, which is the only proven way of increasing participation. However, we need urgent action and, with the Bill before us today, we have an ideal vehicle to introduce compulsory voting, which would have an instant impact on democratic participation.

When the Secretary of State introduced the Bill in the Commons, he said that the Government should leave our democratic system in a better place than we found it. The Bill will do this in many ways, but we must do better with regards to turnout. Registered turnout in every election since 2001 has been below 70%, and turnout fell below 60% in 2024. Given gaps in registration, the IPPR estimated that this was only 52.8% of all eligible adults, making this the lowest effective turnout since universal suffrage. That is why we need compulsory voting.

More than 22 democracies, including Australia, Belgium and Brazil, use this system. In Australia, where it has been in place since 1922, turnout is typically over 90%. The arguments for compulsory voting are overwhelming: it is the only measure proven to raise voting levels over the long term; it is popular with the British public, as evidenced by polling; it increases participation among younger and poorer voters, making election outcomes more representative; it is policy-led, as parties are forced to persuade middle-ground voters, rather than simply focusing on getting the vote out, which, in turn, reduces the cost of elections; and it is balanced, because politicians are motivated to work towards greater consensus, as appealing solely to political bases is disadvantageous when elections do not depend merely on turning out the party faithful.

I agree with the IPPR’s argument that compulsory voting is a key step towards rebuilding civic trust and countering populist claims of a failed system. If my noble friend is not able to agree to the amendment, I would ask her to ensure that the national commission on electoral reform, as it looks at what changes are needed to make sure that our democracy wor

title: Local Healthcare Availability
text:
Mr Bayo Alaba (Southend East and Rochford) (Ind): 6. What steps she is taking to help ensure that high-quality healthcare is available to people closer to where they live.

The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Yvette Cooper): It is important that people get the highest quality of healthcare closer to where they live. That starts with improving access to GP care. As a result of the work we have done, there are now 24 million additional GP appointments a year compared with before the election, and we have now announced neighbourhood care reforms, including new neighbourhood support teams, to help the frailest of patients stay well and safe at home.

Mr Alaba: In recent months I have been deeply impressed by the way healthcare providers in Southend East and Rochford, including North Shoebury surgery, have thought outside the box to deliver proactive and patient-focused services. What measures is the Department putting in place to ensure that this sort of high-quality care is available to people closer to their homes?

Yvette Cooper: The hon. Member is absolutely right about this: we know that some people end up in emergency care because they could not get early enough support and care at home. That is why we are giving GPs £40 million this winter to identify the frailest patients and put in place home care plans, and from next April, we will roll out new neighbourhood support teams to help the frailest 1% of the population across the country. This is a fundamental change in the way that we provide NHS care, and will provide those patients with support and care in their own homes.

Rishi Sunak (Richmond and Northallerton) (Con): As an ambassador for Prostate Cancer Research, I support local testing events in communities up and down the country, including a very successful one in my own constituency this weekend, organised by Wensleydale Rotary club. Does the Secretary of State agree that community groups play a vital role in raising awareness of and testing for prostate cancer, and will she join me in thanking those groups, including Rotary, the Lions and the Graham Fulford charitable trust, and the medical volunteers for all their efforts, which are saving men’s lives from community to community?

Yvette Cooper: I thank the right hon. Member for his advocacy and campaigning on prostate cancer, which affects so many men across the country. As he will know, the Government will roll out England’s first targeted prostate cancer screening programme, as recommended by the UK national screening committee. We have asked the committee to keep the programme under continual review. Men who are not covered by the screening programme and who are concerned can also talk to their GP about getting a prostate-specific antigen test based on informed choice. He is right that raising awareness about prostate cancer is critical, and many campaigning organisations do an amazing job on that.

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text:
The Minister of State, Department for Work and Pensions (Baroness Sherlock) (Lab): My Lords, with the leave of the House, I will now repeat a Statement made by my right honourable friend Stephen Timms in the other place. The Statement is as follows:

“With permission, I would like to make a Statement on the final report of the Timms Review of Personal Independence Payment. Personal independence payment provides vital support to deaf and disabled people, and people with long-term health conditions. It contributes to the additional costs they face, and aims to help them live independently, participate in their communities and, in some cases, to work.

PIP was introduced 13 years ago. Since then, there have been many changes, but PIP has never been fully reviewed and has not kept pace, so the Timms review was launched in summer last year. The review was co-produced with disabled people, the organisations that represent them and other experts. It is the first time that the UK Government have co-produced a review of this scale. I want to express heartfelt thanks to my two co-chairs, Sharon Brennan and Dr Clenton Farquharson, and to the 12 steering group members whom the three of us recruited from more than 340 applicants. The group has met for a full day on 15 occasions since January, with lots of other discussions in between. The whole group has shown exemplary commitment to the task.

Each of the 15 members, including me, had one vote. Almost all 12 of the steering group members had lived experience of disability or long-term ill health, as well as a range of other expertise. The review heard from more than 40,000 people and organisations. That included over 38,000 responses to the call for evidence, 138 community workshops, and evidence from clinicians, charities, deaf and disabled people’s organisations, academics, front-line practitioners and international experts. I thank everyone who shared their expertise and their experiences—often deeply personal—with us.

This was an ambitious review. It asked big, complex questions. Co-production means that every participant does not necessarily agree on every detail, but we created the conditions for people with different perspectives to test the evidence and shape the outcome as equals. The review’s report has been submitted to the Secretary of State and the Government will now consider its findings.

Let me turn to the review’s central conclusion: the system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset. The review is clear that PIP remains a vital source of support but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It does not consider people’s needs, aspirations, barriers or extra costs—it is just about what someone cannot do. Many find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and it too often leaves people fearing that work, treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it.

Secondly, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution towards the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey, reviewed by the steering group, showed that PIP does not always target the highest levels of support at those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions reflecting individual circumstances better.

Thirdly, the system offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.

The review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not an exercise in adjusting forms or descriptors. It does not prescribe a final set of eligibility rules, because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected Government, accountable to this House, but it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made. Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly. The highest support should reflect the most severe needs. Substantial further work is needed. The Government will undertake this work, and we will set out our

title: Maternity Services: St Helier Hospital
text:
Luke Taylor (Sutton and Cheam) (LD): 5. What steps she is taking to help improve maternity services at St Helier hospital.

The Minister for Secondary Care (Karin Smyth): I have met a number of Members to discuss the issue of maternity services at St Helier hospital, where we are committed to ensuring safe, high-quality care. The board at the hospital is considering the safest option to address the water and estates challenges. Of course, maintaining patient safety and staff safety must be the highest priority. I understand that the trust board is making a decision at the beginning of December.

Luke Taylor: I thank the Minister for meeting me and colleagues at very short notice to discuss ways to keep maternity services accessible for my constituents due to further failures at St Helier hospital. She knows that the water safety issues in the women’s health block mean the trust is facing difficult and expensive decisions and that, at the same time, lift failure has closed the paediatrics block and the re-ablement unit has been closed due to structural failures. I know the Minister understands the urgency of our pleas, but it would be remiss of me not to take every opportunity to ask that she redoubles efforts to work with the Treasury so that we can bring forward our new hospital, which will secure women’s health and maternity services in Sutton and deliver a brand-new, world-leading hospital for our patients.

Karin Smyth: The hon. Member is quite right: it would be remiss of him not to advocate on behalf of his local trust, as many Members do. Further to the Secretary of State’s comments, the state of the estate that we inherited after the last 14 years is well documented. We have put the new hospital programme on a sustained footing, and we have ensured there is money allocated to it, which was not the case when we came into power. The capital budget is on a longer-term, sustainable footing. I am happy to continue to meet Members across the House to get these hospitals built quickly and on time for the patients they are designed to serve.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text:
Northern Ireland, Scottish and Welsh legislative consent sought. Relevant documents: 12th Report from the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee, 4th Report from the Constitution Committee.

Clause 17: Registration without an application

51A: Clause 17, page 24, line 5, leave out “or an overseas elector’s declaration” Member's explanatory statement This amendment seeks to probe whether auto-enrolment can also be applied to British overseas voters.

Lord Jamieson (Con): My Lords, my Amendment 51A concerns auto-enrolment of British citizens who are entitled to vote but are resident overseas. In 2024, it was estimated that only around 200,000 of the approximately 3.5 million British citizens abroad were registered. Of that, around half actually cast a vote. Less than 6% were registered and less than 3% voted in the 2024 election. If we really care about democracy and representation, surely we should not ignore these citizens.

While there are practical issues around databases, as we highlighted in the proposal to introduce automatic registration as a whole, we should not ignore this group. This is a probing amendment; if it is appropriate to have auto-registration for British citizens within the UK, then it should be appropriate for all British citizens. Why do we treat this group of electors as second-class citizens? Why do we not put the same effort into enabling these electors to register and vote? These are the principles behind the amendments tabled by me and my noble friend Lady O’Neill of Bexley.

Amendment 66 would enable a system whereby overseas citizens would have the opportunity to register to vote whenever they renew their passport. It is a practical suggestion to increase voter registration. Amendment 118 would allow overseas voters to vote in person at a British embassy, high commission or consulate. This would make voting more accessible. Particularly in countries where democratic elections are not the norm, we could proudly showcase democracy and how voting can be done. More broadly, our Amendment 119 would require an independent review into increasing the registration and participation of overseas electors in UK parliamentary elections.

Recent changes to the system of registering have caused problems. For instance, the renewal process is not user friendly, and the registration process does not direct applicants to choose a voting method. Also, typical delivery times for a letter from Europe are around five working days, but they can be longer, particularly for smaller towns. For locations further afield, such as Dubai and New York, they are seven to 10 days, and in other places they take even longer. Given that postal ballots are generally sent out only 10 to 15 working days before an election date, in practical terms postal ballots will work only within Europe. Even then, that is dependent on the elector immediately filling out their ballot paper and returning it without delay, and having no delays in the postal system. In the 2024 election, return rates were 75% for France but only 32% for Spain and 6% for Australia. What work are the Government doing to improve this system and ensure that such a large portion of the electorate is not disenfranchised?

As we have said, citizenship matters regardless of your place of residency. People live overseas for a variety of reasons; it does not mean they have any less right to vote than any other citizen. I thank the British Overseas Voters Forum for the engagement we have received regarding the difficulties of overseas voters registering and the practicalities of voting. I hope the Minister will take our suggestions on board. I look forward to hearing what other noble Lords have to say and their recommendations in this area, which has been overlooked for too long. I beg to move.

title: NHS Reorganisation
text:
Peter Fortune (Bromley and Biggin Hill) (Con): 4. What progress she has made on the reorganisation of the NHS.

The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Yvette Cooper): Subject to passage of the Health Bill, NHS England will be brought back into the Department of Health and Social Care next April. My statement on 4 November set out the next steps for how those changes will be delivered, but the purpose of the reforms is to help us get back to what the NHS does best—caring for people where they need it most—and ending the duplication and fragmentation of our national health service system.

Peter Fortune: I thank the Government for their reversal of the abolition of Healthwatch and local Healthwatch organisations, and I pay tribute to Charlotte and Helen at Healthwatch Bromley because it has been very unsettling for them. With the support the Government are now giving, will the Government agree to a minimum funding standard to account for the different size of Healthwatch organisations across the country?

Yvette Cooper: I agree with the hon. Member that Healthwatch plays an important role across the country. That is why I took the decision to ensure that Healthwatch, and so the local patient voice, can continue. We are also strengthening the voice for patients and the focus on patient experience at the national level, with a new director in post. He will know that the funding decisions also reflect the allocations and ICB allocations, but I hear his point.

Marsha De Cordova (Battersea) (Lab): I am pleased to see the Government making progress on NHS reorganisation. The all-party parliamentary group on eye health and visual impairment recently published its report, which found that only just over 3% of blind and partially sighted people found the NHS app to be fully accessible and inclusive. As the Government continue to make progress on moving from analogue to digital, does the Secretary of State agree that it is vital they ensure the voices of disabled people are part of that reorganisation? Will she also agree to meet me to discuss how we can remove some of those barriers, and has she received a copy of my report?

Yvette Cooper: I welcome my hon. Friend’s point. We clearly need to improve digital access to NHS services across the country. Those reforms are moving at pace and are making the NHS much more accessible, but she is absolutely right that all other ways to access GP services have to exist and that we must ensure that all reforms are as accessible as possible. I would be happy to follow up directly on her specific points.

Sir Jeremy Hunt (Godalming and Ash) (Con): The Amos review identified 748 recommendations to improve maternity safety, but the body responsible for implementing those recommendations—the National Quality Board—is chaired by NHS England, which is being abolished from next April. Will the Health Secretary confirm that the NQB will continue, will be co-chaired by the Care Quality Commission and will not just catalogue recommendations, but will actually decide on them with a person and a date by when they will be implemented?

Yvette Cooper: The former Health Secretary makes an important point about the challenge of recommendations that are never implemented. We are setting up a new hub within the Department to keep track of recommendations, some of which are duplicates and some of which contradict each other. We will shortly be setting out a first action plan on maternity services based on the work of the maternity and neonatal taskforce. We also expect the National Quality Board to continue.

Clive Efford (Eltham and Chislehurst) (Lab): Following the abolition of NHS England, what arrangements will replace the patient voice function of the specialised blood disorders clinical reference group, and how will organisations representing people with haemophilia and other bleeding disorders be involved in specialist commissioning decisions?

Yvette Cooper: My hon. Friend makes an important point. I can tell him that we are setting out many of the specialist commissioning functions, which will continue to be done at a national level. It is important that that takes place alongside the expansion of strategic commissioning by ICBs. We expect patient voice to be taken into account at every level when it comes to commissioning, and we are strengthening the patient voice directly in the Department as well as part of these reforms.
